title: A Time for Everything
overview: The writer reflects on life's changing seasons, God's timing we cannot fully grasp, injustice, and the death that comes to everyone.

parts.label: A time for everything (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: Fourteen pairs of opposites sweep across all of life, including hard ones like killing and hating. The point is not that each one is good, but that life moves through these turns on a timing we do not set.

parts.label: Beautiful, but beyond us (vv. 9-11)
parts.note: After the list, the writer asks what all our effort really gains. He says God has made each thing fitting in its time and placed a sense of the eternal in people, though the Hebrew word is debated and no one can see the whole picture.

parts.label: Enjoy life as a gift (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: His answer is to be glad, do good, and enjoy food and work as gifts from God, whose work lasts and invites awe. Verse 15 says history repeats itself, and its last line is hard to translate, possibly meaning God brings back what has passed or holds it to account.

parts.label: Injustice in the courts (vv. 16-17)
parts.note: The writer sees wrongdoing in the very places meant for justice. He tells himself that God will judge everyone in the end, because judgment also has its time.

parts.label: Humans and animals die alike (vv. 18-22)
parts.note: Looking only at death, he says people and animals share the same breath and return to the same dust. He openly asks who knows whether the human spirit rises, and settles again on enjoying one's work, since no one can see what comes after.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the bleak lines about death, such as verse 21, are the writer's real doubt left open or a view he raises in order to answer it with hope in God's coming judgment.
think: Which is harder for you to live with: not knowing why things happen when they do, or not knowing what comes after death?
